items.title: aiohttp server lacks an initial request/header timeout
items.description:
### Summary

The keepalive timeout was not used during the initial portion of a request.

### Impact

An attacker could keep an idle connection open indefinitely before sending any data.

### Workaround

Use a reverse proxy (as recommended for all production deployments) with sensible keepalive limits.

items.title: AIOHTTP: Secure attribute not enforced for shared cookie
items.description:
### Summary

The Secure attribute was not being enforced for the shared cookie.

### Impact

It may be possible to send a shared cookie marked Secure through an unencrypted request.

items.title: aiohttp: Multiple instances of excessive or unbounded memory/CPU use
items.description:
### Summary

Multiple cases were found where aiohttp could use excessive or unbounded memory, or excessive CPU consumption on attacker controlled requests.

### Impact

An attacker could cause resource exhaustion through specially crafted requests.

items.title: russh: Unbounded memory allocation in agent protocol server via crafted constraint records
items.description:
### Summary

`russh_keys::agent::server::add_key` (`russh/src/keys/agent/server.rs:271-319`) spawns a dedicated tokio task for every 5-byte `SSH_AGENT_CONSTRAIN_LIFETIME` record attached to an added key, each cloning the key blob and sleeping for the declared lifetime (up to ~136 years). The loop has no per-request task budget, and spawned tasks are not rolled back when the overall request fails. Repeating one constrained add-key message over an agent connection converts wire bytes into resident tasks and heap at roughly 141x amplification: in our measurement 10.2 MiB of protocol traffic produced ~2,096,120 live tasks and +1,447,856 KiB RSS, while the same traffic sent as unconstrained add-key requests cost +268 KiB. items.title: A russh SSH server accepts a publickey authentication whose signature uses a different algorithm than the one named in the request
items.description:
### Details

In `russh/src/server/encrypted.rs`, `server_read_auth_request_pk` (0.63.3, around lines 880-990):

* The requested algorithm name (`pubkey_algo`) is read and only used to decode the key: `PublicKeyOrCertificate::decode(&pubkey_algo, &pubkey_key)`. The derived `hash_alg` is then dropped (`PublicKeyOrCertificate::PublicKey { ref key, .. }`).
* The signature blob is decoded (`Signature::decode`) and verified with `Verifier::verify(&pubkey, &buf, &sig)`. `ssh-key` picks the hash from **the signature's own algorithm** (`sig.algorithm()`).
* `pubkey_algo` and `sig.algorithm()` are never compared.

So for an RSA key, the request can say `rsa-sha2-512` while the signature is `ssh-rsa`. The signature is valid for SHA-1, verification succeeds, and `Handler::auth_publickey` is called.

items.title: Mercury: Stored / DOM Cross-Site Scripting (XSS): mr.Markdown renders untrusted content as raw, unsanitized HTML
items.description:
## Summary

Mercury turns Jupyter notebooks into shared web apps/dashboards. The `mr.Markdown`
widget converts its input to HTML with **python-markdown and no sanitization
step**. `MarkdownWidget` is an `ipywidgets.HTML` widget, whose value is written to
the page as **raw HTML (via `innerHTML`) with no sanitization**, so the result
reaches the DOM verbatim. When an app passes **untrusted data** (database rows,
user submissions, uploaded file contents, or an external/LLM API response) to
`mr.Markdown`, HTML/JS in that data executes in the browser of **whoever views the
app** — a data-driven stored/DOM-based XSS.

This is a library-provided rendering sink that fails to neutralize output; it is
triggered by ordinary, reasonable application code, not by an author mistake.

## Root cause

`mercury/md.py` — `MarkdownWidget._to_html()` (verified at v3.2.6, lines ~57–65):

items.title: Mercury: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in /api/terminals - access control bypass
items.description:
### Summary
A missing comma in `mercury_app/block_handler.py`'s `BLOCKED_PATTERNS` list causes the blocklist to fail to cover the `/api/terminals` endpoint. As a result, any unauthenticated attacker can spawn a full, interactive OS-level shell on the host running Mercury.

### Details
The blocklist in `mercury_app/block_handler.py` is defined as:
```
BLOCKED_PATTERNS = [
    # JupyterLab UI + API
    r"/lab(?!/(?:extensions/|api/settings(?:/|$)|api/translations(?:/|$)))(?:/.*)?"
    r"/api/terminals(?:/.*)?",
    r"/api/shutdown(?:/.*)?",
    r"/files(?:/.*)?",
]
```
The missing comma between the first and the second line causes Python to merge the rules, therefore the actual list that is blocked looks like this:

/lab...(?:/.`*`)?/api/terminals(?:/.`*`)? (the first two lines joined together)
/api/shutdown(?:/.`*`)?
/files(?:/.`*`)?

items.title: agent-router: MCP session resume does not verify the embedded anti-hijacking subject; default Helm seed makes session IDs forgeable
items.description:
## Summary

The MCP proxy's client-facing session ID embeds the authenticated caller's
subject (JWT `sub` claim) specifically as an anti-hijacking discriminator —
matching the Model Context Protocol specification's documented session-hijacking
guidance (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/security_best_practices#session-hijacking).
However, the session-resume path never checks that discriminator against the
current caller's identity, so any client that obtains a session ID (its own or
another user's) can resume that session and act with it — including on
routes with per-user backend sessions. This is aggravated by the official
Helm chart shipping a literal, publicly known default seed
(`"default-insecure-seed"`) for the key that encrypts these session IDs.

## Impact

An attacker who obtains (or, under the default seed, forges) another user's

items.title: Graphify Fortran extractor: incomplete cpp #include hardening allows arbitrary host-file read/exfiltration when indexing an untrusted repo
items.description:
## Summary

The Fortran extractor's C-preprocessor step (`graphify/extractors/fortran.py`, `_cpp_preprocess`) applies an incomplete `#include` hardening. The `-nostdinc -I /dev/null` flags it relies on (comment "Security (F-007)") do **not** stop a capital-`F` Fortran source file from including **absolute paths** (`#include "/etc/passwd"`) or from **path-traversing out of the corpus** (`#include "../../../../home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa"`). `cpp` always searches the directory of the file being preprocessed for quoted includes and always honours absolute include paths, regardless of `-nostdinc`/`-I`. As a result, indexing an untrusted repository that contains a `.F`/`.F90`/`.F95`/`.F03`/`.F08` file reads arbitrary local files off the host and inlines their contents into the knowledge graph, which is then shipped to the LLM/agent and written to the on-disk, shareable output (`graph.json`, `GRAP

items.title: Mercury: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution via /api/kernels
items.description:
Mercury runs a JupyterLab server with **anonymous access by default** (`mercury_app/__main__.py` sets `--IdentityProvider.token=''` when no `--token`/`MERCURY_TOKEN` is given; when tokenless it also sets `--ServerApp.disable_check_xsrf=True`). It relies on a **blocklist** (`mercury_app/block_handler.py` `BLOCKED_PATTERNS`: `/lab`, `/api/terminals`, `/api/shutdown`, `/files`) to keep anonymous users off dangerous Jupyter endpoints.

## The vulnerability
`/api/kernels` is **NOT** in the blocklist (and cannot be — Mercury needs kernels to run notebooks), and `patch_kernel_websocket_handler()` (`mercury_app/idle_timeout.py`) only tracks the idle-timeout: it wraps `on_message` to call `self.application._timeout_manager.touch()` and then invokes the original handler with **no filtering of `execute_request`**. items.title: LoopX serve-status permissive CORS policy exposes control-plane state and private Markdown files
items.description:
## Summary

`loopx serve-status` sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on **every** response,
including its unauthenticated `GET` routes. Because the endpoint is unauthenticated and
bound to a fixed, well-known loopback port, **any website the operator visits can read
LoopX control-plane state and the contents of Markdown files inside every registered goal
repo**, using a plain `fetch()` with no user interaction.

The write endpoints are *not* affected — they are correctly Origin-checked. This report is
strictly about the **read** paths.
